summary: Discovery for air-gapped on-prem deployment. Customer requires fully offline updates, HSM integration, strict RBAC/SSO controls and audit logs. Main risks: hardware constraints in older data centers, maintenance windows for offline updates, validation of quantized models in their compute environment. Redwood AE/SE covered architecture options (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private) and proposed Private air-gapped workflow plus next steps to size and validate a pilot.
topics: Air-gapped upgrade process and offline package delivery
KMS/HSM and encryption key management in air gap
Approved hardware profiles (GPUs/TPUs) and quantization effects
Fallback and rollback (canary, A/B) in offline environments
transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood - I'll hand off to Ethan for the technical side in a bit. Uh just to confirm we have Lisa, Raj, Tom and Sophie on the line?
[00:00:10] Lisa Moreno: Yep, hi Maya, thanks.
[00:00:12] Raj Khatri: Raj here.
[00:00:14] Tom Alvarez: Tom.
[00:00:16] Sophie Blake: Sophie, ML Ops.
[00:00:18] Maya Chen: Great, quick agenda: understand your security requirements and infra constraints, talk through our Private on-prem air-gapped offering, and capture next steps. Ethan, over to you.
[00:00:30] Ethan Patel: Thanks. So Guardian, you're looking to run models fully on-prem, air-gapped, with restricted internet egress, correct? And the goal is to push updates as managed packages rather than continuous pulls?
[00:00:45] Lisa Moreno: Correct. We are in a regulated health vertical, PHI touches some of these pipelines so we need full control. Our legal team requires no outbound connections from the inference nodes.
[00:00:55] Raj Khatri: And to add, we need HSM-backed key management, strict SSO via our IdP, RBAC for model access, and immutable audit logs for any model changes.
[00:01:06] Ethan Patel: Makes sense. We support an air-gapped Private deployment pattern where the control plane can be customer-hosted and update artifacts are delivered as signed bundles that you can import from an offline medium. We also support KMS/HSM integration — we've worked with AWS CloudHSM, Thales, and Azure Key Vault HSM partners, but on-prem HSMs are common.
[00:01:26] Tom Alvarez: How do updates work? Our ops team has tightly controlled windows and we can't just open the network for a registry pull.
[00:01:32] Ethan Patel: Right — we provide a tarball/OCI bundle that is cryptographically signed. You download to an air-gap staging box, validate signatures with your HSM or internal CA, and then we have a scripted install to distribute to nodes. We also provide a dry-run validation for model compatibility and a checksum report.
[00:01:50] Lisa Moreno: Any auto-scaling in that mode? We do want the ability to scale for batch jobs but not have it require internet control plane.
[00:01:58] Ethan Patel: Autoscaling inside your cluster is fine — the orchestration runs locally. The only piece that usually involves Redwood is the management plane for rollouts and analytics, which in air-gapped mode can be run on-premise or optionally via a dedicated control-plane in your VPC. If strict air-gap is required, the control-plane can be fully on-prem with no outbound telemetry. That said, you lose some cloud-hosted convenience features.
[00:02:18] Sophie Blake: How about model telemetry and quality monitoring? We need quality regression alerts but can't send prompt payloads offsite.
[00:02:26] Ethan Patel: We have an on-premizable evaluation agent: it runs locally and stores evaluation metrics in your DB. For external alerting we can send only aggregate metrics or nothing; everything's configurable.
[00:02:36] Raj Khatri: Encryption at rest and key rotation cadence? We need rotation every 90 days and proof of rotation logs in the audit trail.
[00:02:44] Ethan Patel: We support rotation via HSM APIs. The rotation operation can be orchestrated by your automation; Redwood's audit logs capture the rotation events if the control plane is on-prem. Our audit format includes timestamps and signature fingerprints.
[00:02:55] Lisa Moreno: Let's talk hardware. Our DC has older racks, limited power per rack, and we can't fit full 600W GPUs in some aisles. What hardware profile works for you?
[00:03:05] Ethan Patel: We've deployed on a range. For high-throughput generative workloads, we recommend 80GB class GPUs (A100/H100 family) but we also support 40GB variants and 8-bit quantized models to reduce footprint. If power is constrained, you can run model sharding across nodes or use CPU-optimized small LLMs for lower latency non-critical tasks.
[00:03:25] Tom Alvarez: We were hoping to reuse our 2080 Ti racks and some older 32GB cards. Is quantization enough to make performance acceptable?
[00:03:33] Ethan Patel: Possibly. It depends on the model family and sequence lengths. Quantization to int8 or int4 plus kernel optimizations helps. We supply quantization profiles and suggestions (per-model) during onboarding. We'll run a sizing exercise with your telemetry. Worst case, you may need to stage a small Dedicated pool of newer GPUs for latency-sensitive endpoints.
[00:03:53] Lisa Moreno: Latency vs cost — can you give an example SLO tradeoff?
[00:03:58] Ethan Patel: Sure. For example, on a 40B model quantized to int8 on 40GB cards you might see single-shot 200–350ms median token latency for short prompts; on 8-bit smaller models you could hit 80–120ms at higher throughput. If you need sub-100ms deterministically, Dedicated newer GPUs or batching adjustments are needed. We'll provide benchmark numbers with your models.
[00:04:20] Maya Chen: Quick commercial note — we have a Private on-prem pricing band and a Dedicated reserved capacity product. For air-gapped private customers there's an onboarding professional services piece for the initial install. We'll put numbers in the pricing template.
[00:04:32] Lisa Moreno: Ok. About SOC2 / compliance docs — can you share evidence of compliance and pen test summaries?
[00:04:38] Maya Chen: Absolutely. I'll send our SOC2 Type II summary and our standard pen-test report. For Private installs we also have a security checklist we share with customers.
[00:04:47] Raj Khatri: SAML/SSO — we need SAML with attribute-based access. Can you map model-level permissions to our groups?
[00:04:54] Ethan Patel: Yes, we integrate with SAML/SCIM for group sync and map groups to roles at the model/route level. In on-prem installs the IdP integration is configured locally. We also support fine-grained RBAC via policy files.
[00:05:06] Sophie Blake: What about model provenance and data lineage for training data? We need to capture model versions and which prompt sets were used for evals.
[00:05:13] Ethan Patel: Our model registry captures version metadata, hashes, and provenance tags. The local eval agent tags evaluation runs with the model hash and prompt-set id; all that is stored locally in your database.
[00:05:25] Tom Alvarez: How are secrets handled during the offline bundle installation? We can't have plaintext keys shipped.
[00:05:30] Ethan Patel: Bundles are signed and encrypted. We recommend wrapping keys with your HSM prior to import; the installer queries the HSM for wrapping operations. Nothing in the bundle contains raw secret material for production.
[00:05:40] Lisa Moreno: Any known gotchas with upgrading model formats or tokenizers in an air-gapped environment?
[00:05:46] Ethan Patel: Sometimes tokenizer updates change tokenization boundaries which affects evals. That's why we provide a dry-run validation that runs your evals locally in a staging namespace so you can compare metrics. Also, for frameworks, ensure your runtime libs match the bundle's expected kernel/driver versions.
[00:06:03] Raj Khatri: Can Redwood run an initial benchmark on our environment? We'd like an on-site or remote run using our test corpus.
[00:06:10] Maya Chen: Yes — our SE can run a benchmark. For air-gapped we'll provide an executable bundle that you run and return the results.
[00:06:17] Ethan Patel: We'll need a small telemetry sample: typical sequence lengths, concurrency, and request size distribution. If you can provide that, I can fill out the sizing spreadsheet.
[00:06:26] Tom Alvarez: We'll pull anonymized traces, should be able to share by end of week.
[00:06:30] Sophie Blake: CSM and runbook — do you provide an on-call rotation template and runbook for patching?
[00:06:36] Maya Chen: Yes, professional services includes runbooks, and we can whiteboard an on-call rotation.
[00:06:40] Lisa Moreno: Network segmentation — are there special ports/protocols we need to open for internal cluster comms?
[00:06:46] Ethan Patel: Typical gRPC and intra-cluster ports; we'll share a minimal whitelist. For completely isolated clusters you can use host-based forwarding and we support deploying the control plane within the same network.
[00:06:57] Speaker 1: (crosstalk)
[00:07:00] Maya Chen: Quick micro-case: a customer in med-dev had a similar air-gap requirement, they used our offline bundle flow and HSM integration; their main blocker was initial GPU memory tuning, which we solved with a canary of 2 nodes.
[00:07:12] Lisa Moreno: Good to hear. That's similar to what we want — a small pilot.
[00:07:15] Ethan Patel: For the pilot we recommend 2 head nodes and 3 worker nodes, with one worker running a modern 80GB card if available, otherwise two 40GB cards in pooled mode. We'll also bring quantized variants to test.
[00:07:30] Tom Alvarez: What's the rollback story if a model causes an outage? Air-gap complicates rollbacks.
[00:07:35] Ethan Patel: We support immutable model artifacts and local canaries. A typical rollback is to promote the previous artifact from your local registry. The installer keeps versioned metadata and we can implement an automated roll-back script that runs locally.
[00:07:50] Raj Khatri: Do you have an attestation or signed provenance we can feed into our audit pipeline?
[00:07:56] Ethan Patel: Yes, each bundle includes a signed manifest with the package hash and signing key id; your HSM can verify signatures.
[00:08:03] Maya Chen: I'll note to include the sample manifest in the follow-up package.
[00:08:08] Lisa Moreno: Timeframe: our executive sponsor wants a pilot in Q4. Is that realistic?
[00:08:15] Maya Chen: Yes, if we can lock down hardware and you can provide telemetry this week, we can aim for pilot in late Q4. There's a PS window for install and validation, typically 3–4 weeks.
[00:08:26] Sophie Blake: For model licenses — we plan to use OSS models but may need a commercial license for some vendor models. How does that work offline?
[00:08:33] Ethan Patel: We can onboard OSS models easily. For commercial models we work with license holders to deliver licensed bundles that respect vendor EULAs; licensing keys are managed locally via your HSM.
[00:08:45] Lisa Moreno: Any encryption in transit within the cluster? We need mTLS.
[00:08:50] Ethan Patel: We support mTLS between components; certs can be issued by your internal CA and rotated per policy.
[00:08:58] Tom Alvarez: What's the minimum disk footprint per node for models + cache?
[00:09:03] Ethan Patel: Depends on model. A 7B model might be ~10–20GB disk after quantization, whereas 70B could be 60–100GB. KV cache and local caching add variable overhead; we usually recommend SSDs with 1.5–2x size headroom.
[00:09:17] Lisa Moreno: Are there any known incompatibilities with our platform — we're running RHEL 8 with custom kernel modules.
[00:09:23] Ethan Patel: RHEL 8 is common; the main requirement is GPU driver compatibility with CUDA runtime versions expected by the bundle. We'll provide a compatibility matrix. If you have custom kernel modules, we'll need to validate in a staging VM.
[00:09:36] Raj Khatri: Pen test windows — we might want to run an independent pen test on the installed stack post-installation.
[00:09:42] Maya Chen: That's fine — we can coordinate and provide guidance for a safe testing window.
[00:09:46] Lisa Moreno: Anything else we should be aware of?
[00:09:49] Ethan Patel: One operational note: clock drift can impact distributed KV cache consistency; ensure NTP or equivalent is configured across nodes. Also, GPU driver updates require coordinated maintenance, we provide patch guidance.
[00:10:05] Sophie Blake: Good note.
[00:10:08] Maya Chen: Ok we'll recap. Action items — Ethan sizing spreadsheet, Maya pricing and security artifacts, Raj provide network diagram, Tom provide approved images. We'll target a technical deep dive next week.
[00:10:21] Lisa Moreno: Sounds good. Thanks team.
[00:10:23] Raj Khatri: Thanks.
[00:10:25] Tom Alvarez: Thanks.
[00:10:27] Maya Chen: Bye all.
[00:10:30] END: (call ended)

Note: transcription includes occasional mis-hears, e.g., 'KV cache' sometimes transcribed as 'K V cash' and product names like 'Redwood Private' may appear as just 'private' in a few spots. References shared during call: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2.pdf, https://redwood.ai/onprem/airgap-checklist.pdf, (sizing spreadsheet link sent after call).
